rationale: B wins because it turns the same launch into sharper assignment desks, especially enterprise procurement: "The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" gives a CIO-trade reporter an actual problem to report, even if the proof bar is high. A is sturdy, but "Post-Adobe, Figma's First Major Launch" smuggles in a "first major" claim the update never gave it and spends too much energy explaining why the angles are distinct. B still needs a facts diet; it won on reporter-usefulness, not clean grounding.
gaps_in_A: "Figma's First Major Launch" and "first major product announcement" are invented. The update says the launch follows the Adobe collapse; it does not say this is Figma's first major anything.
"That's a different company than Adobe would have built" is boardroom fan fiction without a quote, document, or analyst source in the update.
"Vercel's v0, Framer, Webflow, Builder.io" may be plausible category context, but none of those competitors appear in the supplied facts. Verify before making them the spine of a pitch.
"Tells You Exactly What Figma Is Selling" overclaims what one $25 add-on seat proves. Pricing is a signal, not a confession under oath.
gaps_in_B: "design-to-code has been promised for a decade and has repeatedly produced unmaintainable output" is outside the supplied facts. It may be true; it is still not grounded here.
"starts emitting code that ships to production" and "asking to write production code" overstate the update. We have React and HTML/CSS export, not evidence anyone will ship it.
"first substantive product move framed against the collapsed Adobe acquisition" invents both firstness and framing. The update gives sequence, not strategy.
"newsjack-detector" is a muddled next step for a launch-angle set. The immediate job is proof collection plus journalist-fit-check; hunting a bigger peg can wait unless the launch hook is too weak.
